📞 Your regular vet: Call during business hours for advice
🏥 Emergency vet clinic: Go immediately if symptoms are severe

science.content: Macadamia nuts contain an unidentified toxin that uniquely affects dogs' neuromuscular system. The compound causes reversible weakness and ataxia in hind limbs, likely through disruption of motor neuron signaling. Unlike many toxins, the exact mechanism remains unknown despite decades of clinical observation. Research by Morton (2002) established the LD50 at 2.4 g/kg. The toxin is heat-stable and present in all forms: raw, roasted, salted, and in baked goods. Symptoms are dose-dependent and typically resolve within 12-48 hours with supportive care (ASPCA, 2023).

toxicityData.minimum: Minimum toxic dose: 0.5 g/kg body weight (mild symptoms)
toxicityData.source: Source: Morton, 2002 — Journal of Veterinary Diagnostic Investigation
toxicityData.example: Example: A 15kg (33lb) dog eating 15g of macadamia nuts (approximately 12-15 nuts) would reach the minimum toxic threshold. A typical nut weighs about 1.2-1.5g.

timeline.description: Early signs: weakness in hind legs, ataxia (wobbly gait), vomiting
Progression: tremors, reluctance to stand, abdominal pain, elevated temperature (up to 104°F/40°C)
Resolution: symptoms typically resolve with supportive care; full recovery expected

faqs.question: Are macadamia nuts toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, macadamia nuts are uniquely toxic to dogs. The exact toxin is unknown, but even small amounts cause weakness in hind legs, vomiting, tremors, and hyperthermia. The minimum toxic dose is approximately 2.4 g/kg of body weight. Most dogs recover within 48 hours with supportive veterinary care.

faqs.question: How many macadamia nuts are dangerous for a dog?
faqs.answer: For a 20kg (44lb) dog, as few as 10-12 nuts can cause symptoms. Smaller dogs may react to just 2-3 nuts. The toxic threshold is approximately 0.5g of nuts per kg of body weight for mild symptoms, with severe symptoms appearing at 2.4g/kg.

faqs.question: How long after eating macadamia nuts will my dog show symptoms?
faqs.answer: Symptoms typically appear within 3-12 hours after ingestion. The earliest sign is usually weakness or paralysis of the hind legs, followed by vomiting, tremors, abdominal pain, and elevated body temperature (up to 104°F/40°C).

faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating macadamia nuts?
faqs.answer: Fatalities from macadamia nut poisoning are extremely rare. The LD50 is 2.4g/kg, meaning a 20kg dog would need to eat approximately 48g of nuts (about 40-50 nuts) to reach dangerous levels. However, even sub-lethal doses cause significant discomfort and require veterinary monitoring.

faqs.question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate macadamia nuts?
faqs.answer: Do NOT induce vomiting unless instructed by a veterinarian. Induction is only effective within 30 minutes of ingestion and can cause aspiration pneumonia. Contact ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for specific guidance based on the amount consumed and time elapsed.

banner.title: My Dog Ate a Mushroom in the Yard: What to Do Now
banner.subtitle: Wild mushrooms can cause fatal liver failure — symptoms are DELAYED 6-24 hours. Do not wait for symptoms. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.

rows.action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — do not wait

steps.title: THIS IS A TRUE EMERGENCY
steps.content: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Amatoxin poisoning has a deceptive delay — your dog looks fine for 6-24 hours while the toxin destroys the liver. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.

steps.title: Collect a Mushroom Sample
steps.content: If safe, collect remaining mushroom pieces (including base/bulb). Place in a paper bag (not plastic). This helps mycologists identify the species and determine toxicity risk.

steps.title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
steps.content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start IV fluids. They will monitor liver enzymes for 48-72 hours. Early treatment is the ONLY effective defense.

steps.title: Prepare for Hospitalization
steps.content: If amatoxin poisoning is confirmed, treatment includes: Penicillin G, Silymarin (milk thistle), N-acetylcysteine, IV fluids, and potentially plasma transfusions. Hospitalization typically lasts 3-7 days.

science.content: Amatoxins (alpha-amanitin, beta-amanitin) are bicyclic octapeptides found in Amanita, Galerina, and Lepiota species. They inhibit RNA polymerase II, halting protein synthesis in hepatocytes. The liver is the primary target because amatoxins undergo enterohepatic recirculation. After ingestion, there is a 6-12 hour latent period, followed by a gastroenteritis phase, a brief false recovery (12-24 hours), then fulminant liver failure with coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and death. Treatment within 12 hours has a 90% survival rate; after 24 hours, survival drops to 30% (ASPCA, 2023).

toxicityData.example: A single Amanita phalloides cap contains enough amatoxin to kill a 10-20kg dog. Partial ingestion is still life-threatening.

timeline.description: Latent phase: dog appears normal. Toxin is being absorbed.
Gastroenteritis phase: explosive vomiting and diarrhea begin. This is the BEST treatment window.
False recovery: symptoms temporarily improve. Owners think dog is healing — FALSE sense of security.
Fulminant liver failure: jaundice, bleeding disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, death without aggressive treatment.

faqs.question: Are wild mushrooms toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Many wild mushroom species are extremely toxic to dogs. The most dangerous is Amanita phalloides (Death Cap), which contains amatoxins that cause irreversible liver failure. Other toxic genera include Galerina, Lepiota, and Cortinarius. Even non-lethal species can cause severe GI upset. ANY mushroom ingestion should be treated as an emergency because you cannot reliably identify species in the field.

faqs.question: How long after eating a mushroom will my dog show symptoms?
faqs.answer: Symptoms from amatoxin-containing mushrooms (Amanita) are DELAYED 6-24 hours. A dog appears fine initially, then develops explosive vomiting and diarrhea. After a brief "false recovery" of 12-24 hours, liver failure begins. By the time jaundice appears, damage is often irreversible. Other species cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 6 hours.

faqs.question: What should I do if my dog ate a wild mushroom?
faqs.answer: Treat EVERY wild mushroom ingestion as a life-threatening emergency. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and admit for 48-72 hour observation with liver enzyme monitoring. Do NOT wait for symptoms — early treatment is the only effective defense against amatoxin poisoning.

faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating a mushroom?
faqs.answer: Yes. Amanita phalloides (Death Cap) has a 50-100% mortality rate in dogs without treatment. Amatoxins destroy liver cells by inhibiting RNA polymerase II. Even with treatment, mortality remains 20-30%. The lethal dose is 0.1mg/kg of amatoxin — a single Death Cap cap contains 10-15mg. Early aggressive treatment (within 12 hours) significantly improves survival.

faqs.question: Can dogs eat store-bought mushrooms?
faqs.answer: Store-bought mushrooms (white button, cremini, portobello) are generally safe for dogs in small amounts. However, they offer little nutritional value and can cause GI upset if fed in large quantities or cooked with butter/oil/garlic. Never assume a field mushroom is safe — only eat mushrooms you purchased from a grocery store.

banner.subtitle: Cooked bones splinter into sharp fragments that can puncture the intestinal wall or cause life-threatening obstruction. This is a mechanical emergency, not a poisoning. Call your vet immediately.

rows.action: 🚨 Vet within 1 hour — hollow bones splinter

steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
steps.content: ⚠️ This is critical: vomiting can cause sharp bone fragments to lodge in the esophagus or puncture tissue on the way back up.

steps.title: Offer Soft Food to Cushion Fragments
steps.content: Feed bread, cooked rice, or canned pumpkin to help cushion small bone fragments and reduce injury risk. This does NOT replace veterinary evaluation.

steps.title: Call Your Vet for X-Ray Assessment
steps.content: Your vet will X-ray to locate bone fragments, assess obstruction risk, and determine if endoscopic or surgical removal is needed.

steps.title: Monitor Stool for 3 Days
steps.content: Watch for: bone fragments in stool (normal passage), black/tarry stool (GI bleeding), inability to defecate (obstruction), or blood. Report any abnormalities to your vet immediately.

science.content: Cooking denatures collagen in bones, making them brittle and prone to splintering. Raw bones contain flexible collagen and are less likely to fragment. When cooked bones splinter, sharp fragments (osteoids) can penetrate the GI wall, causing peritonitis — a life-threatening infection. The most common sites of perforation are the esophagus (if swallowed improperly), stomach, and ileocecal junction (where the small intestine narrows). Poultry bones are especially dangerous because they are hollow and shatter into needle-like shards (AAHA, 2023).

toxicityData.minimum: N/A (mechanical hazard — any size fragment can cause damage)
toxicityData.ld50: Not applicable — physical trauma, not chemical toxicity

faqs.question: Why are cooked bones dangerous for dogs?
faqs.answer: Cooked bones become brittle and splinter into sharp fragments. These shards can: (1) puncture the esophagus, stomach, or intestinal wall, (2) cause life-threatening peritonitis, (3) create intestinal obstruction, or (4) become lodged in the jaw or throat. Raw bones are safer because they are more flexible, but cooked bones are NEVER safe.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms if my dog ate cooked bones?
faqs.answer: Symptoms of bone-related injury include: vomiting (possibly bloody), diarrhea (may contain blood or look black/tarry), abdominal pain (hunched posture, reluctance to move), difficulty defecating, excessive drooling, pawing at mouth, and lethargy. Symptoms may appear within hours or be delayed 1-3 days if a slow obstruction develops.

faqs.question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate cooked bones?
faqs.answer: Do NOT induce vomiting if your dog ate cooked bones. Regurgitating sharp bone fragments can cause additional damage to the esophagus or become lodged in the throat. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for immediate guidance.

faqs.question: What is the treatment for bone ingestion in dogs?
faqs.answer: Treatment depends on severity: (1) If bone is lodged in throat/mouth — manual removal under sedation. (2) If bone is in stomach — endoscopic retrieval. (3) If obstruction or perforation — emergency surgery. (4) If small, softened pieces — monitoring with bread/bulk diet to cushion passage. X-rays or ultrasound determine the approach.

banner.title: My Dog Ate Plastic: What to Do Now
banner.subtitle: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause dangerous intestinal blockage. Risk depends on the size and shape of the object. Call your vet if the piece is larger than 2cm.

decisionGuide.safe: Plastic piece smaller than 2cm (e.g., corner of wrapper). Monitor stool for 48 hours.
decisionGuide.call: Plastic piece 2-3cm OR your dog shows ANY vomiting/lethargy. X-ray may be needed.
decisionGuide.emergency: Plastic larger than 3cm, OR persistent vomiting, OR no bowel movement in 48 hours. Surgery likely needed.

steps.title: Assess the Ingested Object
steps.content: If possible, find the remaining pieces and measure them. Was it a wrapper, toy piece, or bag? Size and shape determine risk.

steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Large or Sharp
steps.content: ⚠️ Large objects can lodge in the esophagus; sharp edges can cause damage during regurgitation. Only induce if instructed by a vet for small, smooth items within 30 minutes of ingestion.

steps.title: Feed a Bulk Meal
steps.content: Offer bread, canned pumpkin, or cooked rice to help wrap the plastic and encourage safe passage. This is NOT a substitute for veterinary care if the object is large.

steps.title: Monitor Closely for 48 Hours
steps.content: Check: Is your dog eating? Vomiting? Defecating? Locate the plastic in stool if possible. Absence of bowel movement for 24+ hours with vomiting = emergency.

science.content: Plastic is chemically inert and non-toxic to dogs — the danger is purely mechanical. The canine GI tract narrows at two critical points: the pylorus (stomach exit, ~1-2cm diameter in small dogs) and the ileocecal junction (small-to-large intestine transition). Objects wider than these passages become lodged, causing a complete or partial obstruction. Complete obstructions cause fluid accumulation, electrolyte imbalances, and intestinal necrosis within 48-72 hours. Surgical intervention is required for objects that do not pass within 24-48 hours or cause persistent vomiting (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).

toxicityData.example: A 2cm plastic toy ball will not pass through a medium-sized dog's pylorus. Objects >2cm require vet assessment.

timeline.description: Assess the object. If small (<2cm), monitor. If large or sharp, call vet immediately.
Small pieces may pass through stomach. Watch for vomiting, lethargy, or abdominal pain.
Critical monitoring window. If no bowel movement AND vomiting = possible obstruction. Seek emergency care.
If still no bowel movement, X-ray needed to locate blockage. Surgery may be required if object is lodged.

faqs.question: Is plastic dangerous for dogs?
faqs.answer: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The danger depends on the size and shape of the plastic object relative to your dog. Items larger than 2cm wide are unlikely to pass through the pylorus (stomach exit) or ileocecal junction. Sharp plastic edges can also cause GI perforation.

faqs.question: Symptoms of plastic blockage in dogs?
faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 2-48 hours: repeated vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, lethargy, abdominal pain, absence of bowel movements, and dehydration. A complete obstruction causes persistent vomiting, dehydration, and shock within 24-72 hours. This is a surgical emergency.

faqs.question: How long does it take for plastic to pass through a dog?
faqs.answer: Small plastic pieces (under 2cm) typically pass through the GI tract within 24-48 hours and appear in stool. Larger items may take 3-5 days or become lodged. If plastic has not passed within 48 hours, or if vomiting occurs, veterinary intervention is required.

faqs.question: When should I call the vet if my dog ate plastic?
faqs.answer: Call your vet immediately if: (1) the plastic object is larger than 2cm in any dimension, (2) your dog vomits more than once, (3) no bowel movement occurs within 48 hours, (4) your dog shows abdominal pain or lethargy, or (5) the plastic piece is sharp/rigid. Do NOT wait for symptoms if the object is large.

emergency: Persistent vomiting with no bowel movement
urgent: Object 2-3cm and not seen in stool after 24h

steps.title: Gather All Medication Information
steps.content: Bring the pill bottle: drug name, strength (mg), number of pills missing. Calculate total mg consumed: strength × pills. This is critical for toxicity assessment.

steps.title: Call Poison Control IMMEDIATELY

steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Professional Guidance

steps.title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination

science.content: Dogs metabolize many drugs differently than humans. NSAIDs (ibuprofen) inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, reducing protective prostaglandins in the GI tract and kidneys, leading to ulceration and renal failure. Acetaminophen depletes glutathione in canine hepatocytes and converts hemoglobin to methemoglobin, impairing oxygen transport. Dogs are particularly sensitive to many ADHD medications (amphetamines) due to their effect on catecholamine release. Even "harmless" supplements like vitamin D can cause fatal hypercalcemia when ingested in large amounts (ASPCA, 2023).

toxicityData.minimum: Drug-dependent: Ibuprofen 50mg/kg, Acetaminophen 75mg/kg, single pill of some ADHD meds
toxicityData.example: A single 200mg ibuprofen tablet can cause kidney failure in a 4kg dog. Five tablets (1000mg) = 250mg/kg = potentially fatal dose.

timeline.description: Best window for induced vomiting. Call poison control before inducing.
Drug absorption phase. Symptoms begin for fast-acting drugs (ibuprofen): vomiting, abdominal pain.
GI ulceration phase (NSAIDs). Symptoms: bloody vomiting, black tarry stool, kidney stress begins.
Organ damage phase: liver failure (acetaminophen), kidney failure (NSAIDs), seizures (antidepressants). Hospitalization required.

faqs.question: Which human medications are most toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: The most dangerous human medications for dogs include: (1) NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — GI ulcers and kidney failure at 50mg/kg. (2) Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — liver damage and methemoglobinemia at 75mg/kg. (3) Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs) — serotonin syndrome. (4) ADHD medications (amphetamines) — severe stimulation. (5) Benzodiazepines — paradoxical agitation. (6) Vitamin D supplements — fatal hypercalcemia.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of ibuprofen poisoning in dogs?
faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 1-4 hours: vomiting (possibly with blood), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. At toxic doses (50mg/kg+): kidney failure (increased thirst/urination, then decreased urine), GI ulceration, liver damage, and seizures. Megaesophagus (enlarged esophagus) can occur with chronic exposure. Treatment includes activated charcoal, gastroprotectants, IV fluids, and blood monitoring.

faqs.question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate medication?
faqs.answer: Inducing vomiting may be recommended if ingestion occurred within 30 minutes and your dog is alert. However, do NOT induce vomiting for: caustic substances, if your dog is already symptomatic (seizures, ataxia), or if the medication is rapidly absorbed. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 with the drug name, strength, and estimated number of pills consumed.

faqs.question: How is medication toxicity treated in dogs?
faqs.answer: Treatment depends on the drug: (1) Induced vomiting + activated charcoal (if early), (2) IV fluids for elimination, (3) Gastroprotectants (omeprazole, sucralfate) for NSAIDs, (4) N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen, (5) Cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, (6) Lipid emulsion therapy for fat-soluble drugs. Hospitalization for 24-72 hours is typical for significant ingestions.

rows.action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — internal bleeding delayed
🚨 Emergency vet NOW — seizures within hours

steps.title: Step 1: This Is a Dire Emergency
steps.content: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Anticoagulant rodenticides have a 2-5 day delay before bleeding begins. By the time symptoms appear, the damage is done. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.

steps.title: Step 2: Bring the Product Package
steps.content: Take the bait package or a photo to the vet. The active ingredient determines treatment: anticoagulants need Vitamin K1; bromethalin needs brain swelling management; cholecalciferol needs calcium-lowering therapy.

steps.title: Step 3: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
steps.content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 1-2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start specific antidotes. For anticoagulants: Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks with blood clotting tests.

steps.title: Step 4: Hospitalization May Be Required
steps.content: Bromethalin poisoning requires 24-72 hour monitoring with mannitol for brain swelling. Anticoagulant cases need plasma transfusions if bleeding is active. Early treatment dramatically improves survival.

science.content: Anticoagulant rodenticides inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), preventing recycling of vitamin K. This depletes active clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), causing spontaneous hemorrhage. Second-generation anticoagulants (brodifacoum, bromadiolone) are 100x more potent than warfarin and persist in the liver for weeks. Bromethalin uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in brain cells, causing cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure. Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) causes hypercalcemia, leading to metastatic calcification of kidneys, heart, and blood vessels (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: Is rat poison deadly to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, rat poison (rodenticide) is one of the most deadly toxins for dogs. There are two main types: (1) Anticoagulant rodenticides (warfarin, bromadiolone, brodifacoum) — prevent blood clotting, causing fatal internal bleeding. Single-dose types require one feeding; multiple-dose types are cumulative. (2) Neurotoxic rodenticides (bromethalin, strychnine, cholecalciferol) — cause brain swelling, seizures, or hypercalcium within hours. Without treatment, mortality rates are 50-90%.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of rat poison in dogs?
faqs.answer: Anticoagulant symptoms appear 2-5 days after ingestion: weakness, pale gums, coughing blood, bloody vomit/diarrhea, nosebleeds, and collapse. Neurotoxic (bromethalin) symptoms appear within 2-24 hours: severe muscle tremors, seizures, ataxia, and paralysis. Cholecalciferol causes kidney failure with increased thirst/urination within 12-36 hours.

faqs.question: Can my dog survive rat poison?
faqs.answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. Anticoagulant poisoning is treatable with Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks; survival rate is 80-90% if treated before symptoms appear. Bromethalin has no antidote — treatment is supportive care (activated charcoal, mannitol for brain swelling) with 50-70% survival if treated early. Strychnine and cholecalciferol also require immediate veterinary intervention.

faqs.question: What should I do if my dog ate rat poison?
faqs.answer: Treat this as a dire emergency: (1) Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. (2) Go to the nearest emergency vet NOW — do not wait for symptoms. (3) Bring the product label to identify the active ingredient. (4) Induced vomiting within 1-2 hours may help prevent absorption. (5) Even if your dog seems fine, delayed symptoms are common and early treatment is life-saving.

steps.title: Step 1: Calculate Total Nicotine
steps.content: Count cigarettes/packages consumed. Cigarette: 10-15mg each. E-liquid: check mg/mL concentration × mL consumed. This determines toxicity risk.

steps.title: Step 2: Call Poison Control IMMEDIATELY
steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Nicotine is absorbed rapidly through oral mucosa — effects can begin within 15 minutes.

steps.title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Symptomatic
steps.content: ⚠️ If your dog shows tremors, seizures, or agitation, inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only induce if instructed by a professional AND your dog is asymptomatic within 15 minutes.

steps.title: Step 4: Go to Emergency Vet for Monitoring
steps.content: Your vet will administer activated charcoal, provide IV fluids, and monitor heart rhythm and respiratory function. Symptoms can progress rapidly.

science.content: Nicotine is an alkaloid that binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in the autonomic ganglia, neuromuscular junctions, and CNS. At low doses, it stimulates receptors causing tachycardia, hypertension, and CNS excitation. At high doses, it causes receptor depolarization blockade, leading to bradycardia, respiratory paralysis, and coma. The biphasic effect (stimulation then depression) is pathognomonic. Dogs metabolize nicotine primarily via hepatic N-oxidation, with a half-life of approximately 1.5 hours. E-liquid poses extreme danger because 1mL can contain 3-24mg of nicotine absorbed rapidly through oral mucosa (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: How much nicotine is toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: The toxic dose of nicotine in dogs is 20-100mg/kg. For a 20kg dog, this equals 400-2000mg of nicotine. Sources: 1 cigarette = 10-15mg nicotine, 1 cigarette butt = 5-7mg, nicotine patch = 8-21mg, nicotine gum = 2-4mg, e-liquid = 3-24mg/mL (highly concentrated). Even ONE cigarette can cause symptoms in a small dog.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of nicotine poisoning in dogs?
faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 15-60 minutes: hypersalivation, vomiting, tachycardia (rapid heart rate), muscle tremors, agitation, and hypertension. As toxicity progresses: bradycardia (slow heart rate), weakness, collapse, respiratory paralysis, and seizures. The biphasic effect — first excitation then depression — is characteristic of nicotine poisoning.

faqs.question: Is vape liquid dangerous for dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, e-liquid (vape juice) is EXTREMELY dangerous due to high nicotine concentration. A single 10mL bottle can contain 30-240mg of nicotine — enough to kill multiple small dogs. The sweet flavorings also attract dogs. Ingestion of even small amounts requires emergency veterinary treatment.

faqs.question: What should I do if my dog ate tobacco?
faqs.answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Calculate total nicotine consumed: mg per item × number of items. Go to emergency vet if your dog ingested: (1) more than 1 cigarette, (2) any e-liquid, (3) a nicotine patch, or (4) any amount if your dog shows symptoms. Do NOT induce vomiting if seizures or tremors are present.

science.content: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) binds to CB1 cannabinoid receptors in the canine central nervous system. Dogs have a higher density of CB1 receptors in the cerebellum (responsible for coordination) and brainstem than humans, explaining their heightened sensitivity. THC is lipophilic and undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, prolonging effects. Edibles are dangerous because the GI tract absorbs THC rapidly, and the liver converts 11-hydroxy-THC, which is 5x more psychoactive. Most cases are supportive — there is no specific antidote, but IV lipid emulsion therapy can accelerate THC clearance (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: Is marijuana toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) is toxic to dogs. Dogs have more cannabinoid receptors (CB1) in the brain than humans, making them significantly more sensitive. Edibles (gummies, brownies, cookies) are especially dangerous due to high THC concentration — one gummy can contain 10-100mg THC, which is toxic to most dogs.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of marijuana poisoning in dogs?
faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: dazed appearance, stumbling/ataxia, urinary incontinence (dripping urine), drooling, dilated pupils, vomiting, tremors, bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypothermia, and in severe cases: seizures or coma. Be honest with your vet — marijuana toxicosis is rarely fatal, and honesty ensures proper treatment.

faqs.question: Are marijuana edibles more dangerous than dried cannabis?
faqs.answer: Yes, edibles are significantly more dangerous: (1) High THC concentration (10-100mg per piece), (2) Often contain chocolate (double toxicity), (3) Faster absorption from GI tract, (4) Dogs eat multiple pieces quickly. Edibles account for the majority of severe cannabis toxicosis cases in dogs.

faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating marijuana?
faqs.answer: Fatalities from marijuana alone are rare in dogs — the LD50 is very high (over 3g/kg of THC). However, edibles pose additional risks: chocolate toxicity, xylitol in some CBD products, and overdose from multiple ingestion. Death is more likely from complications (aspiration pneumonia, hypothermia) or combined toxins. Always seek veterinary care.

faqs.question: Should I tell my vet my dog ate marijuana?
faqs.answer: Yes, always be honest. Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Knowing your dog ate marijuana ensures they provide appropriate care: inducing vomiting (if early), activated charcoal, IV fluids, thermoregulation, and monitoring heart rate. Without this information, your dog may undergo unnecessary tests or receive inappropriate treatment.

steps.title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval

science.content: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) that triggers a rapid, exaggerated insulin release from canine beta cells — up to 6-7x the amount released by glucose. This is because dogs metabolize xylitol via the same pathway as glucose but with different kinetics. The resulting hypoglycemia (blood glucose <60mg/dL) causes neurological dysfunction, seizures, and death. At higher doses (>0.5g/kg), xylitol causes acute hepatic necrosis through ATP depletion and oxidative stress. The mechanism is dose-dependent and unique to dogs — cats appear to be less susceptible (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Xylitol is toxic to dogs at doses as low as 0.1g/kg for hypoglycemia and 0.5g/kg for liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1.0g of xylitol — meaning ONE piece can cause severe hypoglycemia in a small-to-medium dog. Emergency treatment is needed even for tiny amounts.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of xylitol poisoning in dogs?
faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 10-60 minutes (sometimes delayed 12 hours): vomiting, lethargy, weakness, collapse, tremors, seizures, and coma — these result from hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Liver failure symptoms (jaundice, coagulopathy) may be delayed 12-72 hours. Even small amounts cause dangerously low blood sugar.

faqs.question: Why is xylitol toxic to dogs but not humans?
faqs.answer: In dogs, xylitol is rapidly absorbed and triggers a massive insulin release from the pancreas — 6-7x more than glucose would. This causes profound hypoglycemia. Humans do not have this insulin response. Additionally, xylitol causes dose-dependent hepatocellular necrosis in dogs through mechanisms not seen in humans.

faqs.question: What products contain xylitol?
faqs.answer: Xylitol is found in: sugar-free gum, mints, peanut butter (some brands), toothpaste, mouthwash, nasal sprays, chewable vitamins, baked goods, ice cream, and "birch sugar" sold as a sweetener. Some brands: Trident, Orbit, Ice Breakers, Eclipse. Always check ingredient lists before giving human food to dogs.

faqs.question: Can a dog survive xylitol poisoning?
faqs.answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. If caught within 30 minutes, induced vomiting prevents absorption. If hypoglycemia has begun, IV dextrose corrects blood sugar. Even with liver damage, aggressive hospital care (IV fluids, liver protectants, plasma transfusions) has 70-80% survival if treatment begins within 8 hours. Delayed treatment has worse prognosis.

banner.title: My Dog Ate Chocolate: What to Do Now
banner.subtitle: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs cannot metabolize effectively. Immediate action is critical — call your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 right away.

steps.title: Call for Help Immediately
steps.content: Contact ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your nearest emergency vet. Time is critical — do not wait for symptoms to appear.

steps.title: Gather Information
steps.content: Note the type of chocolate (milk, dark, baking), estimated amount consumed, and your dog's weight. This helps the vet assess toxicity risk.

steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
steps.content: Inducing vomiting can cause aspiration pneumonia or worsen the situation. Only do so if explicitly instructed by a veterinarian.

steps.title: Monitor Symptoms Closely
steps.content: Watch for vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, increased thirst, rapid breathing, and seizures. Symptoms may appear within 2-4 hours.

science.content: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, both methylxanthines that dogs metabolize much more slowly than humans. While humans eliminate theobromine in 2-3 hours, dogs take 17.5 hours or more. This allows toxic levels to build up in their system. Theobromine affects the central nervous system, cardiovascular system, and smooth muscles. At high doses, it causes seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially death (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: How much chocolate is toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Toxicity depends on the type of chocolate and your dog's weight. Milk chocolate becomes toxic at approximately 0.5 oz per pound of body weight. Dark chocolate is 2-3x more toxic. Baking chocolate is the most dangerous — as little as 0.1 oz per pound can be lethal. Use our toxicity calculator to assess your dog's specific risk.

faqs.question: How long after eating chocolate will a dog show symptoms?
faqs.answer: Symptoms typically appear within 2-4 hours but can be delayed up to 12 hours. Early signs include vomiting, diarrhea, and restlessness. Severe symptoms (seizures, irregular heartbeat) may appear 6-12 hours after ingestion. Theobromine is absorbed slowly, so symptoms can worsen over time.

faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating chocolate?
faqs.answer: Yes, chocolate can be fatal to dogs. The lethal dose of theobromine is approximately 100-500 mg per kg of body weight. For a 20kg (44lb) dog, this equals roughly 200g of milk chocolate or 100g of dark chocolate. Immediate veterinary treatment significantly improves survival rates.

faqs.question: How many grapes are toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: The toxic dose is not established, but as few as 1-2 grapes can cause kidney failure in some dogs. Raisins are more concentrated and thus more dangerous. There is no known safe amount — any ingestion should be treated as an emergency.

faqs.question: How long after eating grapes do symptoms appear?
faqs.answer: Vomiting and diarrhea typically begin within 6-12 hours. Signs of kidney failure (decreased urination, lethargy, loss of appetite) may not appear until 24-72 hours after ingestion. Early veterinary intervention is critical.

faqs.question: Why are grapes toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: The exact toxic mechanism is still unknown. Tartaric acid is the suspected toxin, with varying concentrations between grape varieties. This unpredictability makes any grape ingestion potentially dangerous.

steps.content: Xylitol acts fast. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately — do not wait for symptoms.

steps.title: Check the Product Label
steps.content: Find the xylitol content (in grams) and calculate your dog's exposure. Note: it may be listed as 'birch sugar.'

steps.content: Your vet will likely induce vomiting (if within 1 hour), start IV dextrose, and monitor liver enzymes for 72 hours.

steps.content: By the time symptoms appear (vomiting, lethargy, seizures), treatment may be less effective. Early intervention saves lives.

science.content: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that triggers a rapid, massive insulin release from the dog's pancreas. This causes blood sugar to plummet within 10-30 minutes. At higher doses, xylitol causes acute liver failure through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Unlike humans, dogs absorb xylitol rapidly and their bodies mistake it for real sugar, triggering this dangerous insulin response (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: As little as 0.1g of xylitol per kg of body weight can cause hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Doses above 0.5g/kg can cause acute liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1g of xylitol — potentially lethal for a small dog.

faqs.question: How fast does xylitol affect dogs?
faqs.answer: Hypoglycemia can develop within 10-30 minutes of ingestion. Liver damage may take 8-12 hours to manifest. Rapid treatment is essential — do not wait for symptoms.

faqs.question: Where is xylitol found?
faqs.answer: Xylitol is found in sugar-free gum, candy, baked goods, peanut butter, toothpaste, mouthwash, and some medications. Always check labels — it may be listed as 'birch sugar' or 'xylitol'.

These compounds cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, forming Heinz bodies — damaged hemoglobin that precipitates inside the cell. The spleen then destroys these damaged cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. This process takes 1-3 days, which is why symptoms are delayed (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: How much onion is toxic to dogs?

faqs.question: How long after eating onion do symptoms appear?
faqs.answer: Symptoms typically develop 1-3 days after ingestion as red blood cells are progressively destroyed. Early signs include weakness, pale gums, and reddish urine. Severe cases can lead to collapse and require blood transfusion.

faqs.question: Are all onion types toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes — all Allium species are toxic: onions, garlic, leeks, chives, and shallots. Garlic is less toxic per gram but still dangerous in quantity. Cooking does not reduce toxicity. Onion powder is the most concentrated form.

banner.title: My Puppy Ate aSock: What to Do Now
banner.subtitle: Socks can cause life-threatening intestinal blockages in dogs. Do not wait — call your vet immediately for assessment and possible intervention.

steps.title: Call Your Vet Immediately
steps.content: Contact your veterinarian right away. Note when the sock was eaten and your dog's size — this determines urgency.

steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
steps.content: Unlike toxins, foreign objects can cause more damage coming back up. Only induce vomiting if your vet explicitly instructs you to.

steps.title: Vet May Retrieve Endoscopically
steps.content: If the sock is still in the stomach (within 12-24 hours), your vet may remove it via endoscopy — a non-surgical procedure using a camera and grabber.

steps.title: Monitor for Blockage Signs
steps.content: Watch for vomiting after eating, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These require emergency surgery.

science.content: Fabric foreign bodies are particularly dangerous because they can become lodged at the pyloric sphincter (stomach exit) or in the small intestine. Once stuck, they cause a complete blockage — nothing can pass, and the intestinal wall may become necrotic (die) from pressure. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, and death without surgical intervention. Puppies and small dogs are at highest risk due to their narrower intestinal diameter (AVMA, 2023).

faqs.question: Will my dog pass a sock naturally?
faqs.answer: Small socks may pass through the digestive tract within 24-48 hours, but this is not guaranteed. Larger socks or those that become lodged can cause life-threatening intestinal blockage. Never wait to see if it passes — consult your vet immediately.

faqs.question: How long after eating a sock will symptoms appear?
faqs.answer: Symptoms of intestinal blockage typically appear within 2-24 hours. Watch for vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These are emergency signs.

faqs.question: What is the treatment for sock ingestion?
faqs.answer: Treatment depends on location and size. Your vet may induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), perform endoscopy to retrieve the object, or conduct abdominal surgery if the sock has caused a blockage. X-rays and ultrasound help determine the best approach.

banner.title: Dog Ate Antifreeze: What to Do Immediately
banner.subtitle: Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) causes rapid kidney failure and death. As little as 1 teaspoon can kill — call your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.

steps.title: EMERGENCY VET NOW
steps.content: Go to the nearest emergency vet immediately. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 en route. Every minute counts.

steps.title: Do NOT Wait for Symptoms
steps.content: By the time symptoms appear, kidney damage may be irreversible. The antidote must be given within 8-12 hours to be effective.

steps.title: Bring the Container
steps.content: Take the antifreeze container to the vet. This confirms the active ingredient (ethylene glycol) and concentration.

steps.title: Treatment Window is Critical
steps.content: Your vet will administer fomepizole (4-MP) or ethanol IV to block metabolism. After 12 hours, treatment is much less effective.

science.content: Ethylene glycol itself is not toxic — it is the metabolites produced by the liver that cause damage. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethylene glycol to glycoaldehyde, then glycolic acid, then oxalic acid. Oxalic acid binds with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that destroy kidney tissue. This process causes metabolic acidosis and acute kidney failure within 12-36 hours. The antidote works by blocking alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolite formation (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: How much antifreeze is lethal to dogs?
faqs.answer: As little as 1 teaspoon (5ml) of antifreeze can kill a 10lb (4.5kg) dog. The lethal dose of ethylene glycol is approximately 4.4ml per kg of body weight. This makes antifreeze one of the most dangerous household toxins for pets.

faqs.question: How fast does antifreeze kill dogs?
faqs.answer: Without treatment, antifreeze is fatal within 12-36 hours. The antidote (fomepizole or ethanol) must be administered within 8-12 hours of ingestion to be effective. After kidney failure begins, survival rates drop dramatically.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of antifreeze poisoning?
faqs.answer: Stage 1 (30 min-12 hrs): drunken behavior, vomiting, seizures. Stage 2 (12-24 hrs): apparent improvement (misleading). Stage 3 (24-72 hrs): kidney failure, severe lethargy, mouth ulcers, coma. Early treatment is critical.

Cats are also obligate carnivores with less capacity to process plant-derived alkaloids. faqs.question: Is chocolate toxic to cats?

faqs.question: Why are cats more sensitive than dogs?
faqs.answer: Cats have lower activity of cytochrome P450 enzymes responsible for metabolizing theobromine. While dogs take 17+ hours to clear theobromine, cats may take even longer. Additionally, cats typically weigh less (4-6kg average), so the dose-per-kg ratio from the same amount of chocolate is higher.

faqs.question: How much chocolate is toxic to cats?

faqs.question: What should I do if my cat ate chocolate?
faqs.answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your vet immediately. Cats are more sensitive than dogs — even small amounts are concerning. Bring the chocolate packaging to identify theobromine content. Do NOT wait for symptoms, as cardiac arrhythmias can be sudden and fatal.

science.content: Onions (Allium cepa) contain N-propyl disulfide and S-methylcysteine sulfoxide. These compounds cause oxidative damage to hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin precipitates). The spleen removes damaged cells, causing hemolytic anemia. Cats are especially vulnerable because feline hemoglobin contains more sulfhydryl groups than other species, making it more susceptible to oxidation. Additionally, cats have lower glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity, reducing their ability to protect red blood cells from oxidative injury. Anemia typically peaks 3-5 days post-ingestion (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).

faqs.question: Are onions toxic to cats?
faqs.answer: Yes, onions are highly toxic to cats — more so than dogs relative to body weight. Onions contain N-propyl disulfide and thiosulfates that cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, leading to Heinz body hemolytic anemia. Cats are uniquely vulnerable because their hemoglobin is more susceptible to oxidation, and they produce methemoglobin more readily.

faqs.question: How much onion is toxic to cats?
faqs.answer: Even small amounts are dangerous. Toxic effects can occur at 5g/kg body weight (about 1 tablespoon for a 4kg cat). Regular consumption of smaller amounts (even trace amounts in baby food or broth) can cause cumulative damage. Raw, cooked, powdered, and dehydrated onions are all toxic.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of onion poisoning in cats?
faqs.answer: Symptoms appear 1-5 days after ingestion: pale or yellow gums (anemia/jaundice), weakness, rapid breathing, reddish-brown urine (hemoglobinuria), vomiting, and lethargy. Heinz body anemia is confirmed by blood smear showing damaged red blood cells. Severe cases require blood transfusion.

faqs.question: Can onion powder hurt cats?
faqs.answer: Yes, onion powder is concentrated and especially dangerous. Even small amounts in broth, gravy, baby food, or treats can cause toxicity. Many commercial products contain hidden onion or garlic powder. Always check ingredient labels before sharing human food with cats.

faqs.question: Is garlic salt/powder dangerous for cats?
faqs.answer: Yes, garlic powder and salt are concentrated forms. As little as 1/8 teaspoon of garlic powder can be toxic to a small cat. faqs.question: What are the symptoms of garlic poisoning in cats?

steps.title: Step 1: Wash Your Cat If Oil Is On Fur/Skin
steps.content: Use Dawn dish soap (cuts oil) to wash off any topical exposure. Rinse thoroughly. Do NOT use water alone — oil repels water.

steps.title: Step 2: Remove From Exposure Source
steps.content: Turn off diffusers, remove oil containers, and ventilate the area. Move your cat to fresh air.

steps.title: Step 3: Call Poison Control
steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Bring the oil bottle — tell them the botanical name and phenol/terpene content if listed.

steps.title: Step 4: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
steps.content: ⚠️ Essential oils have high aspiration pneumonia risk. Vomiting can cause oil to enter lungs. Go to vet for safe decontamination.

science.content: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A6 and UGT1A9) enzymes required for phase II glucuronidation of terpenes (d-limonene, alpha-terpineol) and phenols (eugenol, thymol). These compounds accumulate in the hepatobiliary system, causing hepatotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Cats also have deficient P-glycoprotein efflux transporters at the blood-brain barrier, increasing CNS exposure. Tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia) monoterpenes cause dose-dependent CNS depression, ataxia, and hypothermia. Even 10mL applied dermally can be fatal in cats (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: Why are essential oils toxic to cats?
faqs.answer: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzymes needed to metabolize certain compounds in essential oils (terpenes, phenols, ketones). This makes them 10x more sensitive than dogs to tea tree oil, citrus oils, eucalyptus, peppermint, and pine oils. Even topical application on skin can cause toxicity if the cat licks it off.

faqs.question: Which essential oils are most dangerous for cats?
faqs.answer: Most dangerous: Tea tree (melaleuca), wintergreen, peppermint, pine, eucalyptus, citrus (limonene, linalool), cinnamon, clove, ylang ylang, birch, and thyme. Tea tree oil is most commonly reported — even 10-20mL on skin can be fatal. Diffusers are also dangerous as cats inhale droplets and groom them from fur.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of essential oil poisoning in cats?
faqs.answer: Symptoms depend on oil type and route: (1) Ingestion: drooling, vomiting, tremors, ataxia, weakness, hypothermia. (2) Skin absorption: lethargy, hypersalivation, liver damage. (3) Inhalation: respiratory distress, aspiration pneumonia. Tea tree oil specifically causes severe hypothermia and ataxia within 2-8 hours.

faqs.question: Are essential oil diffusers dangerous for cats?
faqs.answer: Yes, diffusers pose three risks: (1) Inhaled droplets settle on fur and are groomed off, causing ingestion. (2) Volatilized oils irritate feline respiratory passages (cats have efficient smell but sensitive airways). (3) Concentrated oil in the diffuser water can be spilled and licked. Use diffusers only in well-ventilated rooms your cat cannot access.

steps.title: Step 1: Check Under Your Cat's Tongue
steps.content: Gently open your mouth and look under the tongue and at the base. Fishing line commonly anchors here. If you see string — do NOT pull.

steps.title: Step 2: Do NOT Pull Any Protruding String

steps.content: Linear foreign bodies often require surgical removal. Your vet will take X-rays, start IV fluids, and perform enterotomy to remove the line.

steps.title: Step 4: Prepare for Hospitalization
steps.content: Post-surgery, your cat will need 2-5 days hospitalization for IV antibiotics, pain management, and monitoring for anastomotic leakage.

science.content: Linear foreign bodies (string, yarn, fishing line) are surgical emergencies in cats. The proximal end anchors — commonly under the tongue, at the pylorus, or in the stomach. Intestinal peristalsis pulls the distal end taught, causing the intestine to plicate (accordion-fold) around it. The taut line exerts pressure on the mesenteric border, causing ischemic necrosis and perforation. Multiple perforations along the intestinal tract lead to septic peritonitis. Unlike dogs, cats have a smaller intestinal diameter and are more susceptible to linear foreign body complications (AAHA, 2023).

faqs.question: Why is fishing line so dangerous for cats?
faqs.answer: Fishing line is a linear foreign body — when swallowed, it anchors at one end (under tongue, in stomach, or at pylorus) while the rest extends through the intestines. Peristalsis pulls the line taut, causing the intestine to accordion-pleat around it. The line then saws through the intestinal wall, causing multiple perforations, peritonitis, and death if not surgically removed.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of linear foreign body in cats?
faqs.answer: Symptoms include: string visible under tongue or protruding from anus, vomiting (especially after eating), drooling, difficulty swallowing, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and fever. CRITICAL: Always check under the tongue and around the base of the tongue — the line may be anchored there.

faqs.question: Should I pull the string out of my cat?
faqs.answer: NO! Never pull on a string or line protruding from your cat mouth or anus. The line may be anchored internally — pulling it can saw through the intestinal wall causing perforations. Go to emergency vet immediately for proper removal under anesthesia.

faqs.question: What is the treatment for fishing line ingestion in cats?
faqs.answer: Treatment requires emergency surgery (enterotomy or gastrotomy) to remove the line. Multiple incisions may be needed along the intestine to release the plicated segments. IV antibiotics treat peritonitis, and fluids correct dehydration. Prognosis depends on how many perforations occurred — early surgery has 80-90% survival; delayed treatment with multiple perforations has 50-60% survival.

article.ogDescription: Emergency guide: What to do if your cat eats lily. Acute kidney failure risk and critical treatment window.

steps.title: Step 1: EMERGENCY VET NOW
steps.content: Go to the nearest emergency vet immediately. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 en route. Time is critical.

steps.title: Step 2: Bring a Plant Sample
steps.content: Take the lily plant or a photo to the vet. This confirms the species and helps assess toxicity risk.

steps.title: Step 3: IV Fluids Are Critical
steps.content: Your vet will start aggressive IV fluid therapy to protect the kidneys. This must begin within 18 hours of ingestion for best outcomes.

steps.title: Step 4: Activated Charcoal May Help
steps.content: If ingestion was recent, your vet may administer activated charcoal to absorb remaining toxins in the GI tract.

science.content: The exact toxic compound in lilies is unidentified, but it causes acute tubular necrosis in feline kidneys. Cats are uniquely susceptible — dogs and humans can eat lilies without harm. The toxin is water-soluble and present in all plant parts: petals, leaves, stems, pollen, and even vase water. Kidney damage begins within hours and progresses to complete renal failure within 24-72 hours without treatment. Early IV fluid therapy (within 18 hours) can prevent permanent damage (ASPCA, 2023).

faqs.question: Which lilies are toxic to cats?
faqs.answer: True lilies (Lilium spp.) and Hemerocallis (daylilies) are highly toxic: Easter lily, Tiger lily, Asiatic lily, Oriental lily, Stargazer lily. Even pollen, leaves, or water from the vase can cause kidney failure. Not toxic: Peace lily, Lily of the Valley (different toxin), Calla lily.

faqs.question: How much lily is toxic to cats?
faqs.answer: Ingestion of as little as 2-3 petals or leaves, or exposure to pollen (grooming pollen off fur), can cause acute kidney failure. There is no safe amount — any exposure requires emergency veterinary treatment.

faqs.question: How long after lily ingestion do symptoms appear?
faqs.answer: Vomiting and lethargy begin within 1-6 hours. Kidney damage is detectable within 12-24 hours. Without treatment, kidney failure develops within 24-72 hours and is often fatal. Early IV fluid therapy is critical.

steps.title: Step 1: Call Your Vet Immediately
steps.content: Contact your veterinarian right away. Note when the string was eaten and how much.

steps.title: Step 2: DO NOT Pull Visible String
steps.content: If string is hanging from the mouth or anus, do NOT pull it. This can cause the anchored end to cut through intestinal tissue.

steps.title: Step 3: Check Under the Tongue
steps.content: If safe to do so, check if string is wrapped around the base of the tongue. If so, this is an emergency — go to the vet NOW.

steps.title: Step 4: Monitor for Symptoms
steps.content: Watch for vomiting, loss of appetite, lethargy, drooling, and inability to defecate. These require emergency surgery.

science.content: Linear foreign bodies (string, yarn, thread, tinsel) are uniquely dangerous because they anchor at one point — typically under the tongue or at the pyloric sphincter — while the rest is pulled through the intestines by normal peristalsis (intestinal contractions). This causes the intestines to bunch up ("pleat") along the string, and the taut string can saw through the intestinal wall like a wire. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and death without surgical intervention. Cats are especially prone due to their barbed tongues that easily catch string (AAFP, 2023).

faqs.question: Why is string dangerous for cats?
faqs.answer: String is a "linear foreign body" — it anchors at the base of the tongue or stomach and the rest is pulled through the intestines as they contract. This causes the intestines to "pleat" (bunch up) and the string can cut through the intestinal wall like a wire, causing perforation, peritonitis, and death.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of string ingestion?
faqs.answer: Vomiting, loss of appetite, lethargy, drooling, visible string hanging from the mouth or anus, abdominal pain, and inability to defecate. If you see string, DO NOT pull it — this can cause more damage.

faqs.question: How is string ingestion treated?
faqs.answer: Treatment depends on location. If the string is still in the mouth/tongue, your vet may cut it. If it has entered the GI tract, surgery is often required to remove it safely. X-rays and ultrasound help determine the best approach.
